newsitem.title: USA: UPS talks recess with no word of strike settlement.
newsitem.headline: UPS talks recess with no word of strike settlement.

text.p: The Teamsters Union and United Parcel Service recessed talks until noon EDT Monday (1600 GMT) with no word of a settlement of the two-week strike by 185,000 employees that has cost the largest U.S. package delivery company $600 million in revenues.
The recess came just hours hours after President Bill Clinton expressed optimism the parties were very close to settling their dispute.
But the Teamsters Union threw cold water on the idea that the parties were anywhere near to settling.
"Reports that a settlement is near are not accurate," the Teamsters said in a recorded message on voice mail. "No agreement has been reached on any major issue."
Only hours before, an optimistic Clinton predicted a deal.

"It's my gut feeling they'll settle," the president told reporters as he arrived at Martha's Vineyard in Massachusetts for a three-week vacation. "They're that close," he said, holding up two fingers not very far apart.
"It's a good deal," Clinton told reporters "It will set a precedent for unions."
But it was not to be, at least not Sunday night.
Soon after the talks recessed, Labor Secretary Alexis Herman canceled television appearances and scuttled plans to fly to California to address the Federation of Government Employees.
It was Herman who convinced the parties to begin talking on Thursday, and who stayed at the hotel throughout the talks. The talks went on, with only brief breaks for sleep, for four days.

On Sunday evening during a brief break, Carey urged his members to keep up the pressure. He spoke in a conference call to more than 200 locals, where rank-and-file members were listening with union officials.

"We still don't have agreements on any major issue," Carey said. He exhorted his members to prepare for everything from candlelight vigils to leaflet distributions at sports events this week to build support for the strike.
Clinton expressed concern on Sunday about the wide-ranging impact of the strike, saying it was "beginning to hurt not only the company but its employees and the people who depend on it."
UPS competitors, including the U.S. Postal Service, have rushed to fill the void. But many small businesses are feeling the pinch of being unable to have their goods delivered.
UPS officials responded to a request by the Federal Reserve Board, sending officials a detailed analysis of the strike's impact on the company and the economy.

Early Sunday, UPS Chairman James Kelly, appearing on NBC's "Meet the Press," sounded an optimistic, though cautious note, saying negotiators were discussing "dozens and dozens of issues" but it was unclear when an agreement could be reached.
"The fact that we're continuing to talk is encouraging," Kelly said, repeating that the company would use replacement workers only as a last resort.
Carey said on the NBC program that the talks had made progress for the first time since they began.
"There has been some movement," he said.
Buoyed by opinion polls showing the strikers winning the public relations battle, Carey stuck to his theme that UPS convert more part-time jobs into higher paying full-time jobs.

For its part, UPS insisted on establishing a new pension fund -- which would cover only UPS workers -- to replace the existing fund covering Teamster workers at dozens of companies, mostly trucking lines.
The strikers were getting help from other unions, but were finding it tough to live on $55-a-week strike benefits.
The strike is the largest since a three-day 1976 strike by 400,000 Teamster truck drivers, according to Cornell University labor studies professor Richard Hurd.
